newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: INTERVIEW - ACPC not going to relax export plan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - ACPC not going to relax export plan.

text.p: The Secretary General of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) said Monday the coffee cartel is not going to loosen its export limit programme despite a recent upward trend in prices.

"We cannot create any feeling that the supply is going to be on a more relaxed mood in the coming months because we need a certain stabilisation of the market," Roberio Oliveira told Reuters in an interview.

ACPC nations have in place a coffee export programme to limit green coffee exports to 53.3 million 60-kg bags between July 1996 and June 1997 compared to its programme a cycle earlier of 45.8 million bags. The basic aim is to limit supply so that prices rise.

Recent market talk had been that the cartel, which groups the globe's biggest producer nations and the 14-member council accounts for more than 80 percent of world production, was looking to modify export plans seeing price trends were largely bullish.

The ACPC, which met over the weekend in in this tiny Central American capital, made no announcements to that affect. The only terse statement the group did make was deemed defensive and cautious by the coffee trade - a stance Oliveira defended.

"We have to be cautious, not only at this time but always, because at the end of the road it is the fate of the producers that is being decided in terms of the impact of supply to the market on the level of price," the Brazilian said.

Asked why the ACPC did not take a more positive stance seeing prices were in their favour with analysts and the trade pointing to the export scheme as the cause, he said the group did not like to boast of its achievements in leading prices. "We are very humble...but we are prepared to implement any measures that members decide," he added.

Oliveira added the figures given out by the ACPC at the weekend technical meeting were aimed at showing that there is a balance in this coffee year between supply and demand in the market. "It is clear to us...that the current level of stocks is something we have to maintain," he added.

ACPC's forecasts have green coffee production for 1996/1997 at 99 million 60 kg bags. "World consumption is increasing, and is now just over 75 million (green coffee equivalent) bags in consuming countries and 25 million bags in producing countries," the group said.
Oliveira disclosed the ACPC's figures for production do not include soluble output. "From the beginning the ACPC has not taken into account soluble output," he said.

Oliveira added he did not see exports from non-members in the coffee year 1996-1997 surpassing those in 1995-1996. "Exports of non-members are not going to exceed those of last year," he said, declining to give numbers. "We have decided not to release numbers, one reason is that we have no control over non-members," he said.

The hands-on head of the group said the reference in the statement to the chairman's powers to call an extraordinary meeting of the full ACPC council was intended to imply that the group is monitoring the market and that the chairman has the mandate to convene a meeting when appropriate to deal with the market.
"It is likely that he will not do it because the market in our view is going to work properly, but if problems arise...," he said, tailing off his sentence wryly.

Responding to criticism that the ACPC gave out no figures for producing nation stock levels, Oliveira said it was impossible to tell what was going on in country stocks because of the lack of regulation to obtain these figures. "But we are going to do a detailed report, country by country, including costs," he said.
Oliveira also declined to say whether the ACPC would implement a third cycle of export limits on the grounds it was too early to tell, but he did hint there would be some kind of follow-through plan.
"We are going to continue, who knows about a third cycle...the idea is to reach a same type of decision by May next year," he said.

On Guatemala's reluctance to ratify the ACPC accord and join the export programme, Oliveira said they were confident that the ACPC could entice the Central American nation back into the fold. "It is a very important country in Central America. They do not have any reason for co-operating."
